title: Pulled elbow
stem: Paediatric area. Ka-yee, 2, won't use her right arm after her father lifted her by the hand to stop her falling on the MTR steps. She holds the arm by her side, slightly bent, palm down. Assess and treat.

phases.title: Assess
phases.goal: The story and the arm: is this a pulled elbow?

phases.title: Reduce
phases.goal: Hyperpronation, then watch her use it.

phases.title: Advice
phases.goal: How to lift her, and when to come back.

notes:
Checked against RCEM/RCH Melbourne guidance on radial head subluxation and the Cochrane review (Krul 2017: hyperpronation more successful than supination–flexion).

Pulled elbow (radial head subluxation, 'nursemaid's elbow'): age 1–4, a pull on the extended pronated arm, the annular ligament slips over the radial head. The child holds the arm still, slightly flexed and pronated, with no swelling, bruising or deformity, and normal shoulder, wrist and neurovascular examination. With a typical history and examination, no X-ray is needed; image if there was a fall, swelling, bruising, deformity, or failure to reduce. Reduction without analgesia: hyperpronation (support the elbow with the thumb over the radial head and pronate the forearm firmly) is first-line; supination then flexion is the alternative. A click may be felt; the child usually uses the arm within 10–30 minutes. Advise lifting under the arms, recurrence risk until about age 5.

Your notes match this, including hyperpronation first.

Perfect script checked against the Cochrane pulled-elbow review, an HKCEM-style scheme and a keyword scheme. Removed the bench's X-ray-first and plaster buttons.

opts.t: Lift her under the arms, not by the hands. It can happen again until she's about 5. Come back if she stops using the arm again.

script.do: Father: I pulled her up by the hand. She didn't fall. None. Arm held pronated and slightly flexed. Mild tenderness over the radial head only.

script.say: Check her hand: perfusion and finger movement.

It'll hurt for a second, then she should start using it again. On your lap, facing me. My thumb over the radial head; with my other hand, I turn her forearm firmly into hyperpronation. A click. Now we watch her reach for a toy.
Lift her under the arms, not by the hands. It can happen again until she's about 5. Come back if she stops using the arm again.
